extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, cooperating teachers, and preservice mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and research-based guidance for cooperating teachers supervising mathematics student-teachers (mentoring practices, feedback, freedom of methods, and discussing instructional goals) drawn from a case study of a difficult internship relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperating teachers should be aware of typical student-intern difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: First, cooperating teachers should be aware of what difficulties student interns are likely to have so they do not find these difficulties to be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the study: time management and understanding student thinking are common difficulties among beginning teachers; knowing these norms can prevent cooperating teachers from overreacting or interpreting normal developmental issues as failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow student teachers sufficient freedom to try ideas from teacher education
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, cooperating teachers should be encouraged to allow student teachers sufficient freedom to try out the ideas they learned in their teacher education programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by conflict over format (PowerPoint requirement) and responsiveness: cooperating teachers may consider certain freedoms (e.g., allowing multiple formats for notes) but such 'freedom' can still be restrictive (e.g., preventing in-class, real-time problem solving). Explicit negotiation about what freedom means is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss philosophies and goals between mathematics educators and cooperating teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Third, mathematics educators and cooperating teachers should be encouraged to discuss their philosophies and goals regarding the student-teaching experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conversations may not produce consensus but can create mutual understanding and help avoid tension (e.g., disagreements about what mathematical topics should receive emphasis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mathematics-specific feedback (not only classroom management feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics-specific feedback is important; feedback that focuses solely on classroom management can cause student teachers to miss opportunities to develop mathematical knowledge for teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers noted mathematics-specific feedback is rare in student teaching experiences. Effective mentoring should include feedback that addresses mathematical pedagogy and content decision-making, not only logistics or management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give timely and ongoing feedback throughout the internship
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid providing little or no feedback late in the semester; consistent, timely feedback throughout the term is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The case study cites Luis receiving little feedback from Sheri late in the semester as a contributor to tension; ongoing feedback supports formative improvement and reduces misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize disruptive interruptions during student lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a propensity to interrupt student teachers during lessons, which undermines their opportunity to respond to students and develop instructional flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interruptions can prevent student teachers from working through in-class problems in real time and from developing responsiveness to student thinking; mentors should balance corrective input with allowing enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify emphasis on mathematical topics between mentor and intern
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiate and clarify which mathematical topics and depth of emphasis are appropriate for the students being taught (e.g., preparing for higher courses versus remediation/consumer-math goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The case shows conflict when a student teacher emphasized domain issues and advanced ideas while the cooperating teacher thought many students would not take calculus; aligning goals reduces tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster positive interpersonal relationships and respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a respectful, non-tense personal relationship between cooperating teacher and student teacher to avoid interpersonal sources of tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tense personal relationship was identified as one of seven causes of tension in the case study; mentoring programs should attend to interpersonal dynamics as well as instructional issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include preparation programs for cooperating teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperating teachers often receive little or no formal preparation; programs should be developed to inform them how to be effective mentors and what to expect from interns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature recommends developing such preparation (Feiman-Nemser, Giebelhaus & Bowman); curricula should cover typical intern difficulties, feedback strategies, negotiating freedom, and aligning instructional goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use design-experiment methodology for instructional intervention development
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing instructional interventions (e.g., the Mayan activity), iterate tasks across cycles of prediction, analysis of student learning, and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Mayan activity tasks were iterated four times across multiple semesters, allowing frequent cycles of prediction, analysis, and task revision as part of a design experiment (Cobb et al., 2003).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote students' reflective thinking about multiple quantifications (ε–N independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction about the limit of a sequence should explicitly promote reflective thinking about the independence of the quantifiers (ε independent of N) and the role/order of variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students often fail to perceive the independence of ε from N; activities should make the logical error of selecting ε dependent on N impossible or transparent (the paper aims to exclude acceptance of arguments like Ben's where ε depends on N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure an intervention with scaffolded steps (Mayan activity three steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement the Mayan activity in three steps: (1) evaluate conflicting student arguments (Sam vs Bill), (2) evaluate the Mayan stonecutter story (tractable analogy), (3) re-evaluate the original statements/arguments to transfer insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2's tractable story helps students map the quantifier-reversal error to a concrete context; Step 3 confirms transfer back to formal mathematical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tractable, transferable contexts (stories/analogies) to reveal logical structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose contexts (e.g., the Mayan stonecutter story) that are easier to track logically but structurally analogous to the mathematical error (reversal of quantifiers), enabling students to perceive the fallacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The priest/craftsman story mirrors the ε–N reversal in Bill's argument and helps students recognize the invalid negation attempt; transferability is key (mapping gap/time to ε/N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tasks to produce and resolve perplexity per Dewey's reflective thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Create learning situations that induce perplexity/confusion and guide students through hypothesis generation, reasoning, and testing to reach post-reflective understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical framing: Dewey's pre-reflective → reflective → post-reflective sequence; Mayan activity intentionally activates students' conflicts with prior beliefs to trigger reflective processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an inquiry-based approach for classes engaging in proof evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an inquiry approach where students make conjectures, verify arguments, and evaluate legitimacy of proofs to support reasoning about limits and quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both studies were run in classes that mainly followed inquiry approaches; such pedagogy encourages students to explore conflicting arguments and reason about logical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using diagrams as a basis for proofs, teach translation to formal proof language
rubrics_metrics.description: If students are to use diagrams and informal visual arguments as the basis for formal proofs, instruction must develop skills to express and justify diagram-based inferences in formal mathematical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers note students struggle to translate visual informal arguments into formal proofs; instruction should include non-trivial proof construction tasks that invite graph/diagram use and explicit practice articulating inferences.
